subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMPLEMENTATION OF LIVESTOCK DIVERSION PROGRAM FOR POTATOES IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMPLEMENTATION OF LIVESTOCK DIVERSION PROGRAM FOR POTATOES IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, because of the interest that has been shown in the House in this matter, I wish to announce that the Agricultural Stabilization Board will implement tomorrow the livestock diversion program recently developed for potatoes in Prince Edward Island. In accordance with the concept of the advance payment, and as I indicated earlier in the House, those who do not wish to participate in this program can obtain possession of potatoes committed to the board by repayment of the advance. The Agricultural Stabilization Board will keep a close watch on supplies and prices, and the extent of the livestock feed program will depend upon the level of producer participation and price reaction.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) for his statement and to congratulate him on acquiescing to the requests of the Prince Edward Island Federation of Agriculture, the potato committee and other interested bodies. I hope, with him, that the program he has announced will prove to be beneficial both to potato growers and to livestock feeders in Prince Edward Island and that any potatoes not diverted but bought back will also be to the advantage of the growers.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF IMPLEMENTATION OF LIVESTOCK DIVERSION PROGRAM FOR POTATOES IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I understand the program undertaken by the government on behalf of potato growers, the government is taking a new approach to that followed up to now. In fact, it is a sort of combination cash payment and storage program, giving the producer the option of either taking his product out or leaving it in. As far as we are concerned, we will be prepared to assess the program when it is finished to see if it has really worked to the advantage and met the needs of the producers. In fact, in the final paragraph of his statement the minister said they will keep a close watch on the program to see how it works out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, NATIONAL STANDARDS GOVERNING ALL POLLUTANTS AND LOANS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
This House expresses the view that in order to protect and preserve our environment, immediate national standards for environmental quality must be set for air, water and land, it being clear that these standards must be set for all pollutants, that they must be enforced by the federal authorities, that low-cost loans



March 21, 1972

must be available to municipalities and to certain industries to ensure no further delay in the building of sewage treatment plants and plant clean-up, and that an Environmental Council of Canada should be established without delay.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to say I have been informed that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) is ill and cannot attend the House today. We regret this, and we trust his recovery will not be long delayed.
I wish to say at the very beginning of my remarks that many more areas of concern could have been included in the motion, for there has been major neglect of environmental problems in every part of Canada over the years. Some progress has been made in this field, but on the whole the record of the federal government has been anything but good. The government had the opportunity to give real leadership in meeting the many environmental dangers facing the nation, but it has failed to meet the challenge. Instead of a national and unified approach to this Canada-wide question, we find that in the field of jurisdiction, environmental standards, control and enforcement there is more fragmentation than ever before.
At a time when the United Nations is calling for a common international outlook and direction, and stressing the need for a unified approach, this government has decided to forgo national standards. It has deliberately passed legislation which may well result in a hodge-podge of different standards from one end of Canada to the other. This short-sighted approach can only result in further delays in effectively meeting the environmental hazards confronting us.
Canada needs an integrated environmental policy. The foundation for such a policy has not been set by this government. The earth as a habitable place for human beings is in serious danger. It is evident that pollution is both widespread and serious. Resource extraction is proceeding at a ruinous rate and our earth is being rapidly overpopulated. All of this amounts to a global situation from whose effects Canada is not exempt. It is obvious that pollution, resource extraction and population are all part of the same picture. Any environmental policy, to be successful, must adopt an integrated approach to the over-all solution.
Our earth can be likened to a spaceship. It is a craft of limited carrying capacity for human beings. The basic elements supportive to life through evolution have developed into systems which constantly recirculate. Complex life-support systems have evolved in which the air, water, nutrients and energy supplies for the inhabitants of earth are normally maintained. Man is so utterly dependent on these natural processes that the policies he devises to govern his actions must ensure their maintenance if he is to survive. Unfortunately this is not being done, and in many parts of the globe there is increasing evidence that man is seriously and dangerously upsetting the balance of nature.
Most of the resources on earth are indefinitely renewable through natural cycles, but some are not. For the continuous provision of high-grade mineral supplies we will have to devise artificial cycles for recovery and re-use. For the exhaustible fossil fuels, such as coal and
Request for Environmental Council
oil, we are developing the alternative of nuclear power, but we must take care that byproducts of heat and radiation do not defeat our purposes by destroying the natural cycles not under our control.
Other sources of energy must be researched and tested, for it is estimated that our resources of oil and natural gas will be pretty well used up within the next 70 or 80 years. This is a pretty sobering thought, especially when you see our present government letting these valuable energy resources go mainly to foreign corporations at fire sale prices. The lack of adequate surveys by government to protect and ensure that future Canadian needs are adequately met in all these fields is most disturbing. The over-all Canadian public interest has not been protected by this government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, NATIONAL STANDARDS GOVERNING ALL POLLUTANTS AND LOANS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. This was amply demonstrated in the field of mineral fuels, which is one of our non-renewable resources. Here, we- find that for the period 1965 to 1968, out of a total of $795 million in book profit, only 5.7 per cent, or $45 million, was classed as taxable income. This disgraceful tax sellout is certainly a source for additional government revenue which might well be used to assist in the clean-up of our environment.
Another disturbing aspect of the environmental problems facing us is the effect which pollution has had on a number of species of wildlife and fish, which are very much a part of our environment. Some species have already been wiped out and an increasing number of species have been reduced to the danger level. This is a clear-cut warning to mankind that many of our activities are adversely affecting the very food chains on which human life on this planet depends. This is the reason that scientists on a world-wide scale are calling for a halt to the destructive pollution of our environment which is presently taking place.
There is one more major point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with briefly before mentioning some of the major environmental problems specifically facing us in Canada. No environmental policy can be effective unless population growth is taken into consideration. Many environmentalists class this as the number one problem facing us in the world today.
The human population of the earth in 1971 is expanding at the rate of 2 per cent each year. This growth rate means that the earth must provide every year for the resources required to support 70 million new individuals. This means providing new food, power, fuel, air, water, minerals, space, doctors, hospitals, teachers, schools, transportation, industrial plants, and countless other cultural resources for a population three and one half times that of the current population of Canada each year. Already there is misery and want in many of the underdeveloped

March 21, 1972
Request for Environmental Council
countries of the world. It is estimated that within the next 30 years the world population could double, and instead of 3.6 billion people on this earth we would then have roughly seven billion people. This means more industry, more resource use, more pollution. The strain on our environment and resources will be immense. It appears doubtful, with this staggering increase in population facing us whether we could ever appreciably increase the standard of living of those people now living in many of the underdeveloped countries in the world.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, every country in the world, including our own, should develop a population policy. I feel Canada should initiate, through the United Nations, international conferences to promote the stabilization of the earth's population. Canada's own population must eventually be stabilized based on the carrying capacity of our environment. Investigations in relation to our per capita needs for all resources should be commenced without delay. I might add that major research on all human settlement problems is also needed immediately. This includes, of course, the increasing number of problems which we are meeting in our rapidly growing urban centres, which currently are the source of most of our severe environmental problems. Long range planning and action on these urban matters cannot be long delayed. There are many other aspects of population growth, but time does not permit me to deal too extensively with them.
Our motion indicates, Mr. Speaker, that our party is interested in the setting of national standards for environmental quality of air, water and land. These standards must be based on the biology of the receiving environment, and not on the purely arbitrary limits of what is technologically possible. If the ecological balance of natural populations or organisms is substantially altered by current technology, then I feel the offending process must be prohibited. National standards must be enforced by the federal authorities and adequate penalties must be set up to ensure compliance with the law. The setting of national standards will force a major clean-up of pollution problems throughout the nation. There is no doubt it will be costly, and for this reason the federal government should be prepared to provide vast sums of money for the over-all clean-up which must come. Low cost loans must be available to all municipalities and to some industries so that they can get on with the job of sewage treatment plants and plant clean-up without any further delay.
A pollution control fund should be established to help tackle some of the most serious and pressing problems facing us. In this category would come the clean-up of the Great Lakes system and other pollution problems which have arisen mainly due to a lack of knowledge and research over the years. The costs of pollution control, however, must be met primarily by the offending party. In some cases subsidies might be necessary, but if so the cost must be made public so the true cost of technology may be assessed. Those who break pollution laws must be liable for the full cost of clean-up, and governments should take steps to ensure that non-recyclable, throwaway consumer products should eventually be phased out by law.
Our party has spoken out on numerous occasions urging the establishment of an Environmental Council of

Canada. The function of the council would be to report on environmental affairs and to give guidance to both the government and the general public on all environmental problems. It would be a non-political organization, with adequate facilities to do a thorough job in the whole field of the environment. The establishment of such a council is long overdue and would be welcomed by Canadians generally.
I indicated earlier that our group is not impressed with the record of this government's attempt to deal with our environmental problems in general. It has been a piecemeal approach at best. A number of departments still jealously guard the right to establish regulations and to dictate policy regardless of the consequences. These ministers cannot do a proper job of protecting our environment if they are constantly in conflict with the commercial and economic aspects of their own departments.
For this reason one over-all Department of the Environment should have been established and should not have been placed in conflict with any economic activity coming under its direct jurisdiction. This is one of the weaknesses of the present Department of the Environment; it has fisheries and forestry under its control. Conflicts of interest do arise. It does not control the whole field of environmental problems and for this reason will often be ineffective in solving pollution problems.
Already in this House we find that we cannot obtain full information from the various ministers on certain important environmental developments. For example, let us look at a major problem in the environmental field in Canada today. I refer to the TAPS versus the Mackenzie River pipeline routes. The public is being kept in the dark. Here we find that several departments are involved, yet no clear-cut policy or clear-cut statement has been madt on the floor of this House as to what is going on in relation to the pipeline or as to what Canadians can expect to come out of it.
Only yesterday, a report indicated that the Americans had released a very voluminous survey which had been made of the TAPS pipeline and the Mackenzie River route. Apparently the United States has far more information, as do the general public in that country, than we in Canada. I think we in Canada are entitled to know just what is going on. What discussions are taking place? What discussions have taken place? If it is envisaged that a pipeline will come down the Mackenzie River corridor, Canadians should know. Is the pipeline being discussed in terms of a common carrier? Who will set the route? Who is going to own the pipeline? What will be the starting point of this pipeline and, when additional finds of oil are made in the Canadian north, will there be room in the pipeline to bring these resources down to the Canadian market? Some members opposite indicate that they have this knowledge. It is not general knowledge throughout Canada, and it is certainly not within the general knowledge of the members of this House.
We are interested in finding out how this pipeline will affect the natives in the north. What plans have been made to make certain that the livelihood of these people, which will be affected by any construction of this type,
March 21, 1972

will be protected? What is being done along these lines? We are also interested in having released the ecological surveys which have been made to indicate whether it is safe for the pipeline to be built. We in the New Democratic Party are very anxious to see this type of information released to this House at the earliest opportunity.
We have opposed the so-called west coast tanker route from Valdez, Alaska, to Cherry Point in the State of Washington. We think it would be disastrous if an oil tanker route were to be established along the west coast. It would be only a matter of time until a major oil spill occurred. We will then see multiplied on an immense scale the disaster which occurred within the past two or three days on the southern shore of Vancouver Island when a ship went aground and many miles of the west coast of Vancouver Island were fouled by the oil which rolled up on the shore.
I would like to make one more point about what we feel has been a lack of policy on the part of this government. We find that the large James Bay project is going ahead. The Quebec government has moved in, surveys have been made and some work has been done. Where does the federal government fit into this picture? This project is part of the over-all environmental problems of this nation but federally we stand on the sidelines because we failed to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. We were ineffective in moving into this area and in demanding that proper ecological surveys be made before the project was allowed to proceed. This is something we should have done in the interest of all Canadians, our environment and our resources. Any Crown corporation should justify the building of dams on any river in Canada. This is what we ask. This is what we are going to press for, and we hope to see amendments of this nature brought forward by this government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, NATIONAL STANDARDS GOVERNING ALL POLLUTANTS AND LOANS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion that is before the House. I think it is obvious that any member concerned with the environment will have to support it. I hope the government will take note once again that the members of this House are vitally concerned about the lack of action in the past two or three years. It is a shame that we have to keep coming back time and again to this subject of the environment. In reply, publicly or in the House, the government says that several pieces of legislation have been passed and surely that is good enough; surely, we cannot be expected to do more. What is wrong with the government's action is twofold.
There are two basic shortcomings in the legislation that we presently have. The first is that the laws have not been passed in a planned or co-ordinated fashion. There seems to be no over-all plan into which the pieces of legislation fit. In other words, they meet a situation or a complaint in some sort of token fashion, but do not form part of a larger plan.
The second failure is that the government has not followed up what legislation it has by regulations and positive action. In these two areas, the government has suggested they have dealt with the situation. One of the failings of the present government is that it feels all that is necessary is to pass laws, get the stuff through the House. The government wants to get bills passed, accepting as
Request for Environmental Council
few amendments as possible, so there will be some indication on the books that the government is concerned. However, that is not enough. It is not the kind of legislation we would like.
Time and again the government refers to pieces of legislation such as the creation of the Department of the Environment, the Canada Water Act and the Clean Air Act, but if you look at the results you find these acts have been completely ineffective up to the present time. When you analyse them, you find they are mainly permissive legislation and in some cases pure token legislation. To a large extent, the goals of an efficient economy and a healthy environment are not contradictory. However, the cost of restoring the health of many sectors of our environment is likely to be very high and the federal government, as the major source of financial power and the broadest forum of Canadian concern for national issues, must demonstrate more leadership in this area than it has in the past.
The government has only been successful in the areas of least resistance. It has hesitated to enter into critical areas for fear of tramping on provincial toes. This, of course, is something about which I am sensitive, coming from the province of Ontario which has a Conservative government and which, like all provincial governments, is very sensitive about its own powers and jurisdiction. In every case in which there has been a move by the federal government, co-operation has been received from the provinces. When proposals are made and plans put forward to the effect that on the Canadian scene we intend to do something about the environment, the provinces co-operate. Time and time again they have co-operated.
The problem is particularly prevalent in respect of the Canada Water Act and the Clean Air Act which supposedly were intended to be the greatest innovative pollution measures in Canada. They have ended up as mere pieces of rhetoric because they hinge on agreements with the provinces before any real positive action can result. As anyone knows, it is no easy matter to bring together a federal government and ten provinces in order to reach agreement. If we look at the various acts, we find there have been no positive results. The so-called national standards in the Clean Air Act apply only in two cases. They apply to any federal premises and can be enforced in the provinces only if the provinces agree.
The Canada Water Act also hinges on federal-provincial agreements. However, on many occasions I have felt extremely sorry that we have been unable to make the Canada Water Act work. From the beginning I felt, as did many others, that it was based on an entirely erroneous premise, and that the whole act would not be effective. If we look at the province of Ontario as the prime example, we find the province already is divided into areas for pollution control. It already has units dealing with pollution control. It has municipal agreements. It has river basin agreements and it has area and regional agreements. This is a pattern which is now completely set up in the province of Ontario. That province has been engaged in this work for 15 years under the Ontario Water Resources Act, but the federal government came along with the Canada Water Act and said that so far as it was

March 21, 1972
Request for Environmental Council
concerned it intended to divide up the area in another way.
So far as the Canada Water Act is concerned, the federal government has said it intends to insist that the matter be handled on a water basin or regional area basis. This has not worked out. There have been a number of agreements with the provinces which show some promise of future activity, but in large part there have been only studies. Studies are fine. However, the problem in respect of the program is that for the first three or four years of its existence most of the time has been spent on studies. Then, when the results of the studies are made known the government is not satisfied with them, finds they did not turn out the way they wished or decides that the studies themselves are ambiguous. Difficult decisions must be made, and yet these decisions have not been made.
Another so-called piece of pollution legislation consists of the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act regarding coastal pollution. Although this act applies to all Canadian waters, it will not be as effective off the west coast of Canada as off the east coast. There are inequities and gaps in the adoption of the regulations under this Act. My colleague, the hon. member for Halifax-Dartmouth East (Mr. Forrestall) intends to deal with this aspect later in this debate, because this is a matter which has concerned him very much, as well as others, and he has been asking questions almost daily on this particular subject.
Another thing I lay at the doorstep of this government as a failure is its inability to make hard decisions. If we look just at the great environmental issues we face at the moment, we will see that this is true. There is a great project for hydro-electric development in the James Bay area proposed by the government of Quebec. There is federal involvement because the closing of navigable waters must be approved by the federal government. There is federal involvement in respect of Indian affairs, environmental affairs and so on. Yet at the moment we have been left completely in the dark concerning where the federal government stands in respect of this project. I recognize that this is not an easy matter with which to deal. The federal government must decide now or shortly whether or not it will agree to this project.
Daily we have been asking, over a period of months now, about the federal involvement in this project and have received no answers. The only inkling we received was in a statement by Premier Bourassa of the province of Quebec. He stated he had been talking to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) about this problem recently. That came out in a news report, but the Prime Minister of Canada has not acknowledged in the House that he has even discussed or considered it. For months we have had nothing but evasive answers. We have not even had an indication that the federal government intends to take the situation seriously and say it is in favour of the project, that it is against the project or that it intends to impose certain conditions. The Prime Minister has not made his position abundantly clear to either the House or to the premier of Quebec.
There is also a decision to be made in respect of the carriage of Arctic gas and oil from Alaska to the mainland of the United States. It must either cross or come close to Canadian soil in such a way that there will be
(Mr. Aiken.]
environmental danger. Yesterday the United States government indicated that a study of this project had been made. A four volume report was tabled at two o'clock yesterday, and the summary we have received is to the effect that the general report indicates there are dangers involved in both routes but that perhaps the overland route is the one that would be most satisfactory to the United States.
This report deals only with the United States. It must decide what is most advantageous for it. The report refers to security-security of the oil passage and security in respect of being able to get that oil regardless of hostile acts from within this country. This is one of the things they are thinking about. I do not know why this aspect has never been considered before. However, a good deal of the report covers the question of security of the oil lines. There seems to be some concern about whether the oil can be moved from Alaska to the United States without any interference from us. I have not seen any evidence that the government of Canada intends to hold public hearings, establish a parliamentary committee to look into the matter, or make a decision.
The special committee on pollution was anxious last year to look into this subject and some hearings were held but nothing final was produced because the committee did not go on a tour as they desired. Perhaps it would have been a good thing to do. In any case, no studies have been made by Canada. When on earth are we going to start, because the Americans are ready to make a decision? They are ready to grant a shipping line permit because that is the easiest and the quickest route, but so far as Canada is concerned it is probably the most dangerous. We do not know whether they are going to make such a decision within days or weeks, but certainly they are going to make it without any indication from this country as to how we feel about it. The decision will be made by the United States strictly on the basis of what they feel will be in the interest of their own security.
There is also the matter of the Great Lakes clean-up. Unfortunately, this work has been stalled, and yet this is a gigantic problem involving two federal governments, one provincial and eight states as well as several other governing bodies. But we have had no decision on that. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, NATIONAL STANDARDS GOVERNING ALL POLLUTANTS AND LOANS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the motion of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) which reads as follows:
This House expresses the view that in order to protect and preserve our environment, immediate national standards for environmental quality must be set for air, water and land, it being clear that these standards must be set for all pollutants, that they
March 21, 1972

must be enforced by the federal authorities, that low-cost loans must be available to municipalities and to certain industries to ensure no further delay in the building of sewage treatment plants and plant clean-up, and that an Environmental Council of Canada should be established without delay.
Mr. Speaker, this motion covers so much ground that it is next to impossible to discuss every aspect of it. Still, I should like to call the attention of the House to that part of it which reads as follows:
-that low-cost loans must be available to municipalities and to certain industries to ensure no further delay in the building of sewage treatment plants and plant clean-up-
Mr. Speaker, the essence of the motion is contained in those lines. I feel that it is imperative that we solve the financial problems of the municipalities to ensure sewage treatment.
Setting up an environmental council, adopting standards and passing laws will be useless if industries and municipalities remain in their present sad situation. We have always said, and I repeat it, that the problem is financial.
Let us hear all the speeches to be made this afternoon and evening, and we will always come to the same conclusion: we are facing a tremendous financial problem. Thus, I would like to draw your attention to a newspaper article published in October 1968 in La Presse and entitled: "Some companies will be unable to survive pollution control". This is what it said:
The federal Minister of Resources, Mr. J. J. Greene, has declared yesterday that some Canadian firms will be compelled to close down because of the government progran on pollution control.
The Minister explained during an interview that pollution was now everybody's problem, but that pollution previously caused by certain industries was their direct responsibility.
The business community must consider the steps that are required to fight pollution as part of the production costs which, needless to say, will ultimately be borne by the population.
Mr. Greene said that Canadians would have to be prepared to accept these additional charges and slightly higher prices as being the cost of living in a healthy atmosphere.
Certain industries may perhaps not be able to pay the cost of pollution abatement measures and will then have to shut down.
"But the federal government understands this point and I think that the public must be prepared to pay for this economic dislocation", said he.
Mr. Speaker, the minister was then suggesting that we should be prepared to pay the cost of pollution abatement, and that certain industries might not be able to foot the bill. He also admitted that the problem was of a financial nature.
In February 1970, I received a letter from Mr. Fowler, President of the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association. This letter related to the federal budget and pollution abatement.
First of all, Mr. Fowler called the minister's attention to the problems for factories which must all tackle the job of not polluting the water and treating it.
And I quote:
-.. the pulp and paper industry solicits that your next budget include the following provisions:
1.	Elimination of federal sales tax on construction materials, equipment and supplies purchased for the purpose of depollution.
Request for Environmental Council
2.	Easing of regulations concerning amortization so that capital expenses directly related to depollution may be amortized over the period most favourable for the firm (the amount to be amortized could be considered as an expense or amortized over any period chosen.)
3.	Federal grants equivalent to one third of capital cost of work carried out to bring existing industrial plants in line with any regulations set up concerning depollution (the government could also allow, instead of such grants, amortization calculated on a broad evaluation of the capital expenditure, having the same financial effect for most companies.)
The above provisions would, in our opinion, facilitate the implementation of depollution called for by various legislation and regulations, among them the Canada Water Act.
I could go on for the rest of the day quoting texts, newspaper articles or statistical data supporting the fact that the problem of pollution must be dealt with, and promptly. I know that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) is aware of the problem and I urge him to give careful consideration, as a possible solution, to low interest loans to municipalities or industries which urgently need these loans and apply for them.
I am surprised to see that a party to my left is supporting this measure and this is gratifying. It proves that all the Social Credit party's interventions to this end have not been in vain. Not so long ago, we were being called all kinds of names when we mentioned interest-free or low interest loans.
I think that municipalities should be entitled to such loans, at least with regard to sewage disposal, and that companies should be able to obtain low interest loans with a much longer write-off period, or even enjoy some tax exemptions.
We will obviously not be talking in terms of thousands of dollars since the problem is of such magnitude that it will require enormous expenses. The main problem is to determine what the federal government is able to do. A brief dated October 26, 1965, by the Canadian institute for the control of water pollution, stated and I quote:
(13) Legislation and tax procedures at the federal, provincial or regional levels should be established and amended so as to insure the most economical and efficient financing of the development, operation and improvement of the facilities for the treatment of sewage waters.
I agree on this point, but towns are facing an even more pressing problem. Industries make profits from which they can deduct tax payments. Actually, most of them are prosperous. But municipalities do not possess the same financial means as a large industry. After all, the damages resulting from unchecked municipal pollution are paid by Canadians.
How can you hope that municipalities like Brompton-ville, Richmond, Windsor, Asbestos, which are all in my riding, can abide by the government's criteria while their budgets show a deficit year after year? How do you expect the resident of Brompton or Windsor to pay higher taxes for pollution control facilities? Actually, these facilities have been totally outrun by budgets 50 per cent of which is earmarked for debt servicing.
The federal government in co-operation with the provincial government should immediately grant interest free loans to municipalities to enable them to deal with pollu-
1008

March 21, 1972
Request for Environmental Council
tion, particularly sewage waters which are discharged into waterways that are frighteningly becoming polluted. The more we hesitate, the more tax money we will have to pay.
I would like that the problem prevailing in the Eastern Townships be considered. In the St-Francois river which runs through my riding at the level of Drummondville, the water does not run any more; it is so polluted by the sewage poured into it by some 120 villages and towns in Quebec that it just rolls down.
A study made by the Quebec Water Board showed that close to 270,000 people live on the banks of the St-Frangois or its tributaries. The river is polluted at East Angus, Sherbrooke, Bromptonville, Windsor and Drummondville. Those towns should stop pouring their waste water into that river and, to that end, the federal government, in co-operation with the Quebec government, should grant those municipalities interest-free loans in order to put an end to such pollution, which is intolerable in 1972.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) for giving me this opportunity to say a few words about the environment, about Environment Canada, about our federal programs and the manner in which these federal initiatives are coordinated effectively with those of the provinces.
His motion expresses the view that, "in order to protect and preserve our environment, immediate national standards for environmental quality must be set for air, water and land." I want to stay close to the main point that he is endeavouring to make. Mr. Speaker, we have been in the process of setting not only national standards but also national objectives.
When I mention objectives I am, for example, talking about the quality of the water out in the middle of a lake, or about the quality of large masses of air over a city. Standards, by contrast, apply to the point of effluence, of pollutants from their source. To repeat, Mr. Speaker, we have already announced a series of national air quality objectives. We have also been announcing a series of standards, which we are working out in close concert with the industries concerned.
We have by no means covered all the industries with which we must work and for which national standards must be set. But in answer to that part of the motion which says that Canada must preserve its environment by setting immediate national standards for environmental quality for air, water and land, I have to say that we are already in the process of doing this. It may take longer to do this job than the hon. member would like to admit. However, we have been working closely with half a dozen major industries.
In two cases we have already announced what these new standards are. These are standards which the industry concerned knows it can meet. They are standards where we have good working examples of pollution abatement procedures being adequate to meet all reasonable tests. They are also economic standards because we can point to plants or mills which are in effect making money and which have installed the necessary clean-up equip-

ment and procedures, and are operating them in an economic way.
The hon. member says that these standards must be set for all pollutants. I will have to agree with him on that. However, it will take us time to work reasonably with the industries concerned to develop a description of the latest working technology. We intend to cover all pollutants, and we will be working with all polluting industries with a view to cleaning up their effluents.
The hon. member also says that these standards must be enforced by federal authorities. Mr. Speaker, he knows very well that the federal authority in many of these fields is not all inclusive. For example, he knows the provinces have specific power over property, and power over the location of many industries. He knows that the provinces have the only powers to deal effectively with local pollution which, in its detrimental influence, does not extend to surroundings which are outside a province, or which does not affect fish, navigation or human health, which are matters of federal concern. There are big areas of jurisdiction in this country which rest exclusively with the provinces.
In those areas, for instance in municipal affairs, in respect to industries located entirely within a province and whose pollutant effects do not go outside the province, it is really the provincial authority that must deal with them. However, having said this, Mr. Speaker, it is our intention, and we have been fairly successful to this point, to develop standards which the provinces will adopt, standards which the provinces will in fact copy, and which they will enforce. Even in areas of exclusively provincial or local jurisdiction we will not have pollution havens which will serve to attract certain "dirty" industries, or will permit some firms to get away with practices which would not be allowed in areas of federal jurisdiction or where the provinces adopt federal standards.
I think the hon. member would also be prepared to admit that where the federal standards are improved upon by a given province or municipality, the federal government should have no reluctance in immediately endorsing enthusiastically those higher standards. It may be that standards are not always uniform across the country. But certainly the national government must be able to set national standards which are uniform in so far as the force and effect of federal laws are concerned and to ensure that those are also standards which are met or exceeded in the provinces and by provincial administrations.
It is proposed in this resolution that low cost loans must be made available to municipalities and to certain industries to ensure no further delay in clean-up. I should certainly like the hon. member to list the "certain industries" to which he would give this preferential treatment. This would be a very interesting exercise, especially so far as the New Democratic Party is concerned. If we are to be selective, what industries should receive financial assistance from the government? In other words, what industries should receive a subsidy from the federal taxpayer in order to clean up?
March 21, 1972

Our basic policy is that the polluter must pay, that the industry in question will have to pay to clean up those wastes which it is now discarding into the environment. This is not an operation involving taxpayers' money or subsidies. It is a requirement which will be imposed upon industry. Admittedly industries often need time in order to bring their plants up to our new standards, in order to instal the latest equipment and use the latest processes which are described in our standards.
In regard to municipalities, the hon. member knows that, in effect, grants have been made to municipalities across Canada for a long time. Most municipalities in Canada have received loans from the federal government, one-quarter of which are forgiveable. If payments are kept up and the plant is in place, then one-quarter of the loan is forgiven at the end of the period. In effect, the municipality in question has received the equivalent of a grant of 25 per cent. Literally hundreds of millions of dollars have been lent to Canadian municipalities over the last decade for this purpose, for the purpose of environmental control, for the purpose of building sewage collection systems and in more recent years the purpose of building primary, secondary and tertiary sewage treatment plants. The Canadian taxpayer, through the federal government, has been helping every municipality that itself had a will to improve its own environment.
Some provinces have seen fit to assist this process. Some, such as Ontario, have made grants to look after those municipalities where the per capita cost is exceptionally high. This is the kind of assistance I mean, but there again we have federal assistance and provincial assistance making it easier for municipalities, certainly those faced with particular problems and high costs, to instal the necessary collection and treatment facilities.
The final point which the hon. member makes is that we should set up an environmental council of Canada. As he knows, this is a big step. We are taking a most important step right away; we are setting up an environmental council of Canada which is appointed by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) and will act in an advisory capacity to him. It is not, at least as initially conceived, a council similar to the Economic Council of Canada which has its own staff, its own civil service so to speak, its own terms of reference and works at its own pace and in its own way. The environmental council which we have in mind and the members of which will be appointed in the next few weeks, will be advisory to the minister. This is a big step; it is a good step and an essential step forward. However, it is only one of a sequence of steps. I might add that I am not personally convinced that we need yet another separate council with its own independent staff, answerable to no one and whose advice is not necessarily practical under the circumstances.
In the few minutes remaining, Mr. Speaker, I wish to take issue with the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Aiken) who said that we really have no philosophy. Essentially, the Department of the Environment is concerned with the preservation of living things, the preservation of wildlife, our fisheries, our forests, our flora and fauna-nature, in other words. This is the mission of ecologists. Indeed, the ecologists are primarily concerned with the inter-relationship of all living things, one to the
25104-5}
Request for Environmental Council
other, particularly with their environments of water, air and soil and particularly again in their relationships with the human animal and what he is doing to them and to his surroundings.
In the Department of the Environment we have many of the biologists who are concerned with the fisheries, who are concerned with the wildlife of this country, who are concerned with forestry. We also have the engineers who are concerned with our waterways, oceanographers who are concerned with ocean currents, the meteorologists who have been sampling air, who are knowledgeable about climatic conditions in this country, about ice movements, about the general backdrop from an air point of view and indeed about inter-relationships between air and water on both our coasts. So, we have the biological competence, the knowhow in this department to endeavour to deal with the impact of industry, of man's building activities on his living environment. It is in that context that we are developing our philosophy of how not only to protect our environment but to improve it as time goes by.
I have made reference to improving the environment and this is entirely possible. It has certainly been possible in the very big field of forestry. Our forests are certainly the biggest wild mass in Canada. They can be healthier if they are harvested. They can produce three or four times as much fibre as they do today. We can have industrialization and we can have a healthier environment and a healthier forest basically because the old, decaying insect-ridden forest which is commonplace in the so-called natural environment will progressively disappear in all but the wilderness and national park areas. In their place will be crops of younger, healthier, fast growing trees. This is a healthier environment, the kind of clean environment that we can have with more industry, and more employment for the people of this country as well.
That is also possible in the fisheries. Somewhat like hunting and somewhat like the ancient practices of the so-called commons, fisheries had been open to everyone. The rush was on and the first in reaped the greatest reward. In time, with the continued invasion of more and more fishermen, the resource itself was in jeopardy. Inevitably, over-fishing occurred; there were too many fishermen, too many boats chasing the remaining fish. Fishing became one of those "bottom-rung-of-the-ladder" type of activities the world over.
Now, we are introducing a degree of order into chaos. Off our shores where other nations are also fishing, we have entered into agreements to reduce our total pressure on the resource. We will share it. Admittedly, we will get 50 per cent or more, but we will share the resource with other countries so long as, collectively, we stay within the total catch. Individually, we will get our share. Once shares are decided on, it will be possible not only to reduce the amount of fishing effort but, as well, to make the fishery much more economical or economically viable. We will be able to withdraw vessels from the fishery or reduce the number of vessels in the fishery, and thus produce much higher incomes for the fishermen left in the fishery. Also, in time, we can build fishing stocks to a level more akin to those which existed before man began

March 21, 1972
Request for Environmental Council
to fish what were formerly extensive fisheries both on our Atlantic coast and the west coast of Canada.
I know that there are many other matters to which I ought to refer. I have said that the polluter must pay. We will, however, give him time to clean up. When he is building a new plant, he must meet the new standards immediately. In cases where there are old, existing plants, he may need some years in order to instal the necessary equipment and processing facilities. That obviously applies to the pulp and paper industry across Canada. There are approximately 150 mills in this country, many of them large, and some of them the largest of their kind in the world. They are not all modern, not all up to date, not all in the best of locations. If we were to force them to solve their pollution problem, or at least meet our new standards for new plants, overnight, many would close down. Certainly, in present circumstances where employment is so important and, indeed, probably the most important matter facing the government of Canada today, we will need to go slowly and put jobs ahead of pollution abatement. We will have to be frank about this and admit this to the country. Time will solve our problems. We shall certainly encourage those mills, one at a time, to meet those reasonable standards which the industry, in the main, agrees are adequate, appropriate, and not too onerous in the circumstances.
I might say in that connection that the United States, for example, is adopting our new standards without change for the pulp and paper industry. Undoubtedly, they will be adopting some of our other standards. We also have established standards for chlor-alkali plants which were discharging mercury. Their effluent has been recycled, the mercury has been recovered, and it no longer finds its way into our rivers and streams. There are other examples one could mention. We are proud when we see other countries following our lead. We, in turn, are learning from them and taking heart from some successes they have scored on the pollution front.
I could enumerate eight different pieces of legislation we have passed in the last two years which deal in a substantial way with pollution. I could list some of the really big developments which I am sure Canadians down through the years will boast about. For instance, who would have thought half a dozen years ago that there would be a firm agreement with the United States for cleaning up the Great Lakes. That agreement has been achieved. I am confident that it will be signed shortly. It incorporates our national objectives for water and will make Lake Erie a lake in which fish can survive and abound. Lake Erie will become a lake that is fit to swim in and its water will be drunk by human beings without any fear of ill effects. That is a massive agreement, a multi-billion dollar agreement, and its scope is impressive. As I say, it is an agreement which will result in the cleaning up of the great water system which drains the industrial heartland of North America. It will result in the cleaning up of that system by the mid 1970's. Mind you, we will be looking for further improvements down through the years. However, Mr. Speaker, that agreement by itself is a tremendous accomplishment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, NATIONAL STANDARDS GOVERNING ALL POLLUTANTS AND LOANS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to listen to the minister and hear what he had to say about the abatement of pollution. Also, I am pleased to support the motion introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding). Certainly, it is high time for Canada to set national standards for the quality of air, water and land.
The minister told us that grants have been given to municipalities for the building of sewage disposal units, etc. This has been done through Central Mortgage and Housing. The amount of funds made available has been small in relation to the need. I am certain that in his motion the hon. member for Kootenay West suggests a program far more expansive than the one operated through Central Mortgage and Housing. The minister is quite right, however, in saying that 25 per cent of loans or funds made available for sewage disposal units, etc., are written off or forgiven if the municipalities meet certain conditions.
The present motion is not unlike one moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) in 1970. At that time the question of pollution was debated. The minister was quite right in saying that a number of pieces of legislation pertaining to pollution have been passed in the last couple of years. However, so far no standards have been laid down. The minister also suggested that there are national objectives or national goals in this area. If there are such objectives, standards, goals or what have you, they are not apparent to Canadian manufacturing firms, Canadian industry generally and to Canadians using our lakes and rivers, our land and air. If there are such objectives and standards, surely they should be made clear to industry across Canada.
In addition, the government's intentions in making sure that these goals are reached should be made clear. It is all very well to say industry is not using land properly and that there shall be penalties. I think the onus today is on the government. It must do a little more in this area. I can think of the difficulties associated with operating mines in the Kenmore district of Alberta. It was suggested that land was being ruined in the area. What have the federal and provincial governments done to assist that industry to repair any damage done to the environment?
I can remember, too, going to Hilton mines in Pontiac county, near Ottawa, a couple of years ago and seeing the huge piles of waste rock heaped up from the iron ore mines. Let me tell the House that the Hilton mines people undertook some expensive research. They wanted to know how much it would cost to flatten out and seed with grass the piles of rock and dust heaped up outside the mine. The experts who were hired said that it would cost $300 per acre. The mining people told the researchers that was too expensive and that they had better come up with some cheaper way of doing it, or forget the whole thing. That experience is not encouraging. That industry should be encouraged to reclaim and repair the sort of damage that is done when open pit mining is undertaking for the recovery of iron ore or coal. Certainly, the government should lay down standards for enabling industry to determine more easily what must be done.
March 21, 1972

It is interesting to note that this motion was moved by a member of the NDP. Members of this House, and particularly of the NDP, have been quick to condemn the Conservative party. They say that it is opposed to advancement and change. The true hallmark of the conservative is that he accepts change based on experience. That is his philosophy. He is not afraid to look back at his mistakes and correct them. If previous governments had done that, perhaps we should not be facing our present difficulties regarding pollution. Mr. Speaker, compare the philosophy of the true conservative with that of the socialist. The socialist, apparently, believes in Utopia. A conservative believes he is the caretaker of the environment on behalf of future generations; he is only here for a limited time and he must take care of our water, air and land so that those who come after him may be able to enjoy it. In order to make this possible one must be prepared to look back and accept change based on experience. I sometimes believe that, over the years, liberal philosophy can be expressed in the question: what will make the biggest buck and the fastest buck in the way most acceptable to industry? Bearing in mind the number of years during which we have had to live with a Liberal government in Ottawa, is it any wonder that pollution is as great as it is today?
The creation of the Department of the Environment was a major step forward. On this side of the House we all regarded it with a great deal of interest. We wondered whether or not the relevant legislation would have teeth in it, whether as guardians of the tax dollar we would be supplied with sufficient information to enable us to judge whether or not the new department was fulfilling a useful service. I was disappointed when the minister told us that the environmental council which is to be set up would report to the department. Such a system will not allow an outside body to check whether the department is acting in an appropriate manner or not, whether it is really cleaning up pollution or whether it is covering up major pollution somewhere or other on the ground that certain industries are involved, or for reasons of good neighbourliness and so forth.
I would much prefer to see an environmental council operated on the lines of the Economic Council and issuing a public report. It could be established on the basis of a mixture of the principles applying to the Economic Council and the Auditor General; it could be, in essence, the auditor of our treatment of the environment; it could audit the management of the environment by the government of the day, and make its report impartially, notwithstanding the effects which the report might have on the government. In this way, it could provide a most useful service. I should like to see the Department of the Environment given increased responsibilities. In my opinion, the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act and the Navigable Waters Protection Act should be placed within the purview of the new department.
Most of our immediate concern arises from the nature of our urban environment. I sometimes wonder how we shall be able to control pollution in large urban areas if we continue to allow cities to sprawl over adjacent territory without limit to their growth. Growing cities do not
Request for Environmental Council
appear to concern themselves greatly over pollution. All one has to do is drive around the major cities of Canada today to realize the extent to which urban sprawl is increasing. The more rapidly cities expand, the less their administrators appear to care about the difficulties of sewage disposal and waste disposal in general.
In the debate which took place last year on this subject the hon. member for Hamilton West listed the percentage of various material which goes into waste. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) referred to the situation in Hong Kong. Reading his speech one can readily understand the difference between the efforts made in Hong Kong to dispose effectively of waste products and those made by various major cities in Canada. There is no doubt, in my view, that cities have been allowed to abuse land surrounding the city area. Standards should certainly be set for municipalities to meet, and, if necessary, grants far larger than have been made in the past should be made available to help them reach those standards. It was said a few years ago that the City of Montreal had installed sewage treatment plants sufficient to handle only about 11 per cent of its raw sewage. This is a shockingly low figure, though I do not wish to single out Montreal as the only example. Other major cities are almost as bad.
We must accelerate existing programs and we can only do this if the government has the courage to lay down specific standards which must be met. In other words, for example, no raw sewage should be dumped into our rivers and waters. If we were as emphatic in making that statement as we are in saying other things, if, for instance, we said that by 1975 no city should be dumping raw sewage into rivers and lakes, then we would see action. Requests for grants would be made to the government and the government would be obliged to come through. But the federal government appears hesitant to take action. It says, among other things, that much of this responsibility lies with the provinces. This may be true to some extent. Nevertheless, over-all authority rests with the federal government, which is responsible for Canada as a whole and the federal government must be prepared to take action to end some of the abuses which have been taking place at the expense of our land, water and air.
So far, the government has taken only what might be called minor initiatives in the area of pollution abatement. Basically it has shown no real leadership. The minister, in his closing remarks, suggested that fish would once again abound in Lake Erie and that after the pact was signed with the United States all the waterways along the Great Lakes system would be cleaned up. But unless a definite commitment is made as to the standard of purification to be met no such result will follow, although the program may have a good appearance for political purposes. Incidentally, there has been a record catch of fish in Lake Erie this year. Results have been far better than last year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL COUNCIL, NATIONAL STANDARDS GOVERNING ALL POLLUTANTS AND LOANS TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House and the country certainly owe a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) for having taken the opportunity today to put forward a motion relating to our environment, thus permitting parliament, at least on this one day, to concentrate its interest upon so important an area. However, because of the way in which parliament functions, because it is controlled by government, and because there is a dictatorship existent in the structure of government activity, not much may come of the complaints which are raised and the propositions which are put forward. None the less, I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West, in taking this opportunity, deserves our applause and the applause of the people in the land. Not one single item is of greater concern to us than the question of the environment, our ecology and living things on the land, in the waters and in the air. Since they are the basis of life, if we do not concern ourselves about them in a serious way we injure the prospect of life on earth continuing beyond a certain point in time.
I listened with a great deal of interest to what the minister said, because after all he is the minister charged with the responsibility for dealing with environmental matters. I should like to extend a word of congratulation to his speech writers. They worked with such care and precision that so far they have prevented the minister from saying anything today on this subject except in general terms, and then not the full truth. When the Department of the Environment was established, and when preceding it a number of other pieces of legislation were announced in speeches from the throne of earlier years, members of parliament had great hopes that we were embarking upon a concrete plan of action to deal with environmental problems, the ecology, and to do something worth while to preserve life in Canada and on shores close to Canada, and thus hopefully influence the situation throughout the world.
For example, as the minister has mentioned we have the Canada Water Act which conceived of the establishment of water management control areas, or river basin boards, or some such bodies as that. I do not know how many have since been established. Has one such water management control area been established, even though the Canada Water Act has been on the statute books for over two years now? I doubt whether any have been set up, but perhaps one has. When the bill was being dealt with by the House, we attempted to establish in the legislation national standards for water quality throughout the nation, so an objective could be set. However, the Liberal party objected to that concept and refused to put into effect national standards.
Then we also had the Clean Air Act. As far as I know, the only activity under that act is that some studies are being conducted into the extent to which our air is being
(Mr. Horner.]
polluted. But in terms of activity and action there has been nothing.
Then, we had the Fisheries Act which again corrected some abuses of the past. This act sought to prevent pollution in the future rather than simply penalize people for pollution after the fact, as had been the case previously. However, when the minister announced the promulgation of the pulp and paper effluent regulations early last November, we found the regulations did not apply to a single, solitary hardboard mill in Canada.
